The impact of these factors on therapy adherence cannot be evaluated. This is one of the limitations of the study. Another limitation of the study is that patients are not randomly assigned to receive treatments, which is a common limitation for observational studies. In the context of paired samples from a large sample, such as hair analysis and urinalysis for detecting cocaine and cannabinoids, the informational yield can be evaluated as follows: 1. True Positives (TP): Cases where both the hair analysis and urinalysis correctly identify the presence of cocaine or cannabinoids. 2. True Negatives (TN): Cases where both tests correctly identify the absence of the substances. 3. False Positives (FP): Cases where the tests indicate the presence of the substances, but the gold standard confirms their absence. 4. False Negatives (FN): Cases where the tests indicate the absence of the substances, but the gold standard confirms their presence. From these categories, several metrics can be derived to assess the informational yield: - Sensitivity (True Positive Rate): TP / (TP + FN) - Specificity (True Negative Rate): TN / (TN + FP) - Positive Predictive Value (PPV): TP / (TP + FP) - Negative PredictivE Value (NPV): TN / (TN + FN) - Accuracy: (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN) These metrics provide a comprehensive understanding of the performance of the paired tests (hair analysis and urinalysis) in detecting cocaine and cannabinoids. For instance, a high sensitivity indicates that the tests are effective in identifying true positives, while a high specificity indicates that the tests are effective in identifying true negatives. The PPV and NPV provide insights into the reliability of positive and negative test results, respectively. In practical terms, the informational yield from these paired tests can inform decisions in various settings, such as clinical diagnostics, forensic investigations, and workplace drug testing. Most motes used for smart grid applications have low power consumption and very short range (less than one meter). texts.full_text: text. This simple premise was the concept behind Berlin-based designer RAN PARK’s latest project: an exploration into how these borrowed terms are used and understood by non-native speakers. The zine features 20 different Konglish phrases that Park has collected over time – some of which he had heard from his own family members, others from friends or acquaintances. The words were then translated back to English in a way that would make sense for native speakers (e.g., “I’m going to the bathroom” instead of “I’m going to take a shit”). Park’s intention was not only to highlight how these phrases are used by non-native speakers, but also to show just how much they can be misinterpreted. The zine is available in both English and Korean versions. The English version features all 20 Konglish words with their corresponding translations; the Korean version includes only those that have been translated back into Korean (i.e., without any of the original Konglish phrases). Park’s work has previously appeared on CoZ, where he discussed his process for creating a series of posters inspired by traditional Korean patterns. Ran Park is an illustrator and graphic designer based in Berlin. He was born in Seoul but grew up mostly outside Korea – first moving to Canada at age 10 before eventually settling down back home again when he turned 23 years old after finishing high school there as well!
